title: AI-native SDLC: how the vendors compare

vendors.name: AWS
vendors.framework: AI-Driven Development Life Cycle, AI-DLC (Jul 2025; FS post May 2026)

anthropic.text: Six stages (Plan, Design, Build, Test, Deploy, Maintain) run as a loop, not a line. Stages are modular; adopt them in any order your dependencies allow.

aws.text: Three phases (Inception, Construction, Operations). Operations feeds production learning back into the next Inception cycle, so it is also a loop.

anthropic.text: Each stage commits a named file (intent.md, spec.md, plan.md, the diff, review findings, incident record). The next stage starts by reading it. The commit chain is the audit trail.

aws.text: AI stores plans, requirements and design artifacts in the project repository so work continues across sessions. Artifact names are not standardised in the posts reviewed.

anthropic.text: CLAUDE.md for conventions, skills for policies applied consistently, hooks for rules that must always hold. All version controlled and reviewed like code.

aws.text: Steering files guide the agent on security policy, architecture standards, approved dependencies and regulatory guidance. Implemented through Amazon Q project rules and Kiro workflows.

anthropic.text: Hooks block or gate actions deterministically (protected paths, test-file edits, production deploys). Managed settings stop engineers switching them off.

aws.text: Enforcement is described mainly as automated quality gates in the CI/CD pipeline and steering files. No equivalent of per-action hooks appears in the posts reviewed.

anthropic.text: Humans review at gates and judge intent and risk. Agentic review layers run first; human review is reserved for regulated and critical code.

links.label: AI in the PR review loop

aws.text: Humans validate each AI plan and decision before execution proceeds. The AI plans, asks clarifying questions, and implements only after human validation, repeated for every activity.

anthropic.text: Autonomy is tiered by environment and risk. Agents act freely in dev, prepare the release in production, and a named person authorises it.

aws.text: Risk-based change categorisation: only material changes need human sign-off, routine changes flow through automated validation. Production and high-impact actions keep approval controls.

anthropic.text: Every session verifies its own work (tests, build, screenshot diff) before a human sees it. Continuous evals regression-test the agent configuration itself.

aws.text: AI validates its own work and self-corrects when tests fail, including deviations from steering files. QA is left-shifted, with high-fidelity test environments and security testing.

anthropic.text: Headless stage: a deterministic detector watches production metrics against control bands and invokes the agent, which writes the finding as a new intent.md. Scheduled security scans and Slack-based on-call extend it.

aws.text: Monitoring feeds the coding agent's context and informs future Inception cycles. AI agents (for example Amazon DevOps Agent) can investigate incident root causes. Less specific on autonomy tiers.

anthropic.text: Not prescribed. Focus is on artifacts, automation and gates. One engineer can run several parallel sessions, but no new team model or vocabulary is mandated.

aws.text: Prescriptive. AI Pods of 2 to 3 developers replace scrum teams of about 7. Sprints become "bolts", epics become Units of Work, and Mob Elaboration / Mob Construction are team rituals. Co-location matters in Inception.

anthropic.text: Each play names a leading and a lagging indicator, mostly read from git history, PR metadata and CI events (for example time from intent to spec, rework after build starts, DORA).

aws.text: A KPI suite (mean time to deploy and recover, failed-deployment %, incidents by severity, technical debt, NPS) plus Amazon's Cost-to-Serve-Software framework for the financial case.

anthropic.text: Dependency graph of twelve plays. Six have no prerequisites, so teams start anywhere and build up.

aws.text: Three-phase adoption: executive alignment, technical enablement, hands-on pilots. States mature DevSecOps must already exist, because AI-DLC amplifies existing capability.

anthropic.text: High. Step-by-step plays with example files, configs, prompts and governance notes for each play.

aws.text: Methodology and principles in the public posts, with the full method in a whitepaper (not yet reviewed here). Open-sourced workflows are available for implementation.

anthropic.text: No customer outcome figures in the playbook itself. It leans on Anthropic's internal practice and the measurement plays.

aws.text: Quotes figures: a Bedrock engine rebuilt by 6 engineers in 76 days against an estimate of 40 engineers for a year, and an unnamed European bank going from 12 to 3 developers. All vendor-reported.

links.label: A signal too big to ignore

bullets: Concrete and implementable: named files, example configs, prompts
Controls are deterministic (hooks, managed settings), not just advisory
Every play has measurable indicators drawn from existing tooling
Modular: start with any no-prerequisite play
Clear operating model for teams (AI Pods, mob rituals)
Strong regulated-industry story: traceability, steering files, risk-based approval
Workflows are open-sourced; the FS post names Claude Code alongside Kiro
Tooling is Claude-centric; other agents need translating
Says little on team structure, roles and change management
No baseline step before the loop; third-party critics flag measurement needs a pre-existing baseline
No customer outcome numbers to anchor an ROI case
Headline results are vendor-reported or unnamed
Public posts are conceptual; detail sits in a whitepaper
Heavy rituals and co-location may be hard to retrofit onto existing teams
Slower on autonomous operation: humans stay close to every plan

third_party.label: Waydev: the playbook's missing layer is measurement
QualityLogic: the playbook is missing one play
ELEKS: AWS AI-DLC explained, with comparisons
